title: Remedial Chaos Theory

jokes.text: ♪Troy and Abed's new apartment!♪ — sung as the door opens
jokes.setup: Guests arrive at the new apartment door and it opens
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed greet them with a jingle about their own apartment, perfectly in sync, as if this is a natural thing to do
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy-and-Abed character comedy — the synchronized jingle is entirely in keeping with their established childlike partnership. It's delightful, requires zero explanation for fans, and sets the episode's warm ensemble tone. Scores high on character integration because only these two would do this, delivered with total sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're moving in, yeah, yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: New place, new adventures!

dialogue.speaker: Troy and Abed
dialogue.line: Troy and Abed in the mooooorning!

jokes.text: Rule number one — dress to impress. Rule number two — avoid touchy topics like the negro problem. The book was written in the '40s.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed announce they read a book on being perfect party hosts and are reciting its rules earnestly
jokes.punchline: Rule two is a casually racist '40s-era social guideline, delivered with complete deadpan sincerity, with Abed footnoting the decade as if that explains everything
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: the earnestness of Troy and Abed following a guidebook, the absurdity of the specific rule, and the perfectly timed deadpan footnote ('The book was written in the '40s') that acts as a straight-faced non-apology. The structure is immaculate — the first rule is innocuous, lowering the guard before the second rule blindsides. Economy is near-perfect. One of the episode's best crafted jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: According to this book on party hosting etiquette, you should never use outdated racist terminology.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What if you just casually mention it with a matter-of-fact explanation?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's still racist, Troy.

jokes.text: Shirley showed up at 3:00. / Time flies when I'm baking. / No, it doesn't.
jokes.setup: Someone mentions Shirley showed up early; Shirley offers the warm cliché that time flies when she's baking
jokes.punchline: Troy flatly contradicts her — 'No, it doesn't' — undercutting the pleasantry with blunt literalism
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic joke. Troy's literal-minded deflation of Shirley's cliché is a solid beat. Character integration is decent — this literalism fits Troy. Not exceptional, but efficiently lands.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Time flies when I'm baking.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No it doesn't. You've been standing there for four hours.

jokes.text: Oh, the door downstairs was propped open with this. This is really unsafe. Anyone could have just wandered into your building. / Like one of our guests?
jokes.setup: Annie presents the propped door as a safety concern
jokes.punchline: Jeff drily points out that the 'wanderers' are literally their invited guests, undercutting Annie's anxiety
jokes.explanation: Solid Jeff retort that characterizes Annie's anxious over-caution. Jeff's sarcasm is well-placed and economical. Not a standout but functional character-driven comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Check this out. I installed a pressure-sensitive floor tile that triggers a rolling boulder mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And here's the golden idol—perfectly balanced so it triggers the trap when you remove it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Adiós, mi amor.

jokes.text: Adiós, Sapito. — the boulder rolls and presumably crushes/scares someone
jokes.setup: Abed's functional rolling boulder exists in the apartment; someone approaches it
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'Adiós, Sapito' — a callback to Raiders of the Lost Ark (Indy's friend Sapito is killed by a dart) — implying the boulder has just 'killed' someone
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character-integrated absurdism. The Raiders reference ('Adiós, Sapito') is an Easter egg for film nerds — it's the name of Indy's doomed guide — delivered with perfect Abed deadpan. This is exactly the kind of hyper-specific, earned absurdist payoff that defines Community at its best. Recurs across timelines, gaining comic weight each time.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed, this Boulder model is incredible! The detail work is just... I mean, wow!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Seriously, it's like you captured the exact essence of Boulder. Every rock, every shadow...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's basically a work of art. Museum-quality. Like, I wouldn't be surprised if someone offered you money for this right now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You guys realize you're doing that thing where you oversell something to make the person feel good, and then you immediately point it out, which somehow makes it worse?

jokes.text: Scale model of the rolling boulder scene from Raiders — with actual rolling boulder. 'Adiós, Sapito.' Annie & Britta: Ahh!
jokes.setup: Abed gives the apartment tour and mentions a scale model of the Raiders boulder scene
jokes.punchline: He triggers an actual rolling boulder (miniature but functional), the girls shriek — the commitment to the bit is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Abed: a deeply specific cinephile reference brought to absurd physical reality. The 'Adiós, Sapito' delivery (quoting Raiders) before triggering it is a perfect character-integrated touch. The girls' genuine reaction grounds it. Visual gag that works on the page and even better on screen. High marks for originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I made a pizza with cauliflower crust, nutritional yeast instead of cheese, and these are sun-dried tomatoes I prepared myself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's great, Shirley.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well? Try it!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Super cool. And sexy. / Super sexy cool. / Overselling it.
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta compete to compliment the boulder display
jokes.punchline: Abed instantly and neutrally calls them out for overselling it
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean beat. Abed's deadpan 'overselling it' is perfectly in character and economically delivered. Gets a mild laugh from the character dynamic but nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Bonjour, Jeff. Je m'appelle Abed-ieu.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's French and Spanish combined. Like our names. Abed-ieu. Get it? A-bed and adieu.

jokes.text: I made pizza. / But we ordered real pizza. / Well, there's nothing more real than homemade. / You didn't have some of the ingredients, so I used ketchup and cream cheese. / We ordered real pizza.
jokes.setup: Shirley announces she made pizza; Jeff pushes back; Shirley defends homemade pizza as more 'real'
jokes.punchline: The reveal that she substituted ketchup and cream cheese for actual ingredients, followed by Jeff's flat repetition of his original objection, now fully justified
jokes.explanation: The repeated line 'We ordered real pizza' works as a bookend, gaining power from the intervening information. The specific choice of ketchup and cream cheese as substitutes is both believable for Shirley's character and disgusting enough to be funny. Well-structured escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wow, Abed. This is a lot of Indiana Jones stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know. I'm a fan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I can see that. You know what this reminds me of? 'Indiana Jones and the Temple of Virgin.'

jokes.text: Oh, look, Indiana Jones and the apartment of perpetual virginity.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just arrived and is reacting to the Indiana Jones boulder display and the general vibe of the apartment
jokes.punchline: He renames the film with a deliberately cruel jab at Troy and Abed's perceived sexlessness
jokes.explanation: Economically vicious. Pierce retools the film title format perfectly — it hits on the Raiders reference, fires at Troy and Abed's manchild living situation, and is entirely in keeping with Pierce's brand of casual cruelty. High quotability. The callback to the boulder gag makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I acknowledge receipt of your insult and have filed it away for future reference.

jokes.text: Banned in Serbia, Jeff. Let that concept sink in.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just told everyone about the banned Serbian rum
jokes.punchline: He repeats it to himself, savoring it — revealing that he's more impressed by his own gift than he's letting on
jokes.explanation: Jeff talking himself into appreciating his own coolness is a good character beat. His self-impressed repetition reveals vanity under the casual exterior. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, your mansion is incredible. How can you possibly complain about it?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, it was built in 1987. That's basically a nursing home for real estate.

jokes.text: Chop busted, fellow adult, chop busted.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just made the 'apartment of perpetual virginity' crack and Jeff responds
jokes.punchline: Jeff ironically validates Pierce's cruelty as 'adult' behavior while noting it as the busting of chops — the 'fellow adult' framing is dripping with condescension
jokes.explanation: Jeff's condescending fraternal sarcasm is well-deployed here. 'Fellow adult' is the key word — it acknowledges and mocks Pierce's self-image simultaneously. Solid if not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, I had him erased from all my family photos. Cost me a fortune at the photo place.

jokes.text: It's nice. Not mansion-nice, but it's nice. / Didn't you used to live in a mansion with me? / Yeah, but this is more my speed and century.
jokes.setup: Pierce backhanded-compliments the apartment and implies Troy is downgrading
jokes.punchline: Troy's comeback — 'more my speed and century' — implies Pierce's mansion is an anachronistic relic, turning the insult back on Pierce's out-of-touch oldness
jokes.explanation: 'My speed and century' is a sharp little retort — implying Pierce lives in a past era is the right counter. Good character integration for Troy showing early signs of standing up for himself.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is Serbian rakija. It's so strong, it's been banned in Serbia.

jokes.text: There's no such thing as Single Malt Platinum Boobs and Billiards Club?
jokes.setup: Abed reveals he fabricated the entire club
jokes.punchline: Jeff's reaction isn't anger — it's genuine, innocent disappointment that the club doesn't exist, revealing how much he wanted it to be real
jokes.explanation: Jeff's sad resignation that his perfect club doesn't exist is a great character moment. The delivery implies he's mourning a dream rather than reacting to being manipulated. Good economy; the specificity of the club name does heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Guys, check it out. I got invited to the most exclusive club in the city.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's amazing, Jeff. How did you manage that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know, right? I must have finally made it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: There's just one thing. That invitation? I made it. On my computer. Last night. As a prank.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The club doesn't exist. I've been planning this for three weeks.

jokes.text: Doesn't bother me. I've hardly missed you at all since I had you removed from my portraits.
jokes.setup: Pierce is responding to Troy's independence; the conversation is about their former living arrangement
jokes.punchline: Pierce reveals he had Troy literally painted out of his portraits — an absurdly aristocratic petty revenge that implies he had formal painted portraits to begin with
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Pierce lines. The joke operates on two layers: (1) the fact that Pierce has formal oil portraits at all is characteristically absurd for his old-money pretension, and (2) the pettiness of having someone removed from them is both hilarious and reveals how hurt Pierce actually is by Troy leaving. Perfect character integration — this line could only come from Pierce. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me I got invited to the 'Competitive Tickling and Interpretive Screaming Club'?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Competitive... Tickling... and... Interpretive... Screaming...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is fake, isn't it?

jokes.text: Check it out. Serbian rum. So strong it is banned there. / Banned in Serbia, Jeff. Let that concept sink in.
jokes.setup: Troy presents a bottle of rum as a housewarming gift
jokes.punchline: The rum being banned in its country of origin is already absurd; Abed's addendum — 'Let that concept sink in' — treats this obvious non-sequitur as a profound philosophical fact
jokes.explanation: The 'banned in its own country' premise is a solid absurdist premise, but Abed's straight-faced instruction to 'let that concept sink in' elevates it. Abed treating this as profound wisdom rather than a marketing gimmick or joke is very much in his analytical character. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I can't believe I fell for that. A guy named 'Buddy Sparkles' sends me an invitation and I just... I never even questioned it.

jokes.text: It was. I made that in Photoshop and mailed it to you a month ago so that you'd keep tonight open on your calendar. / There's no such thing as single malt platinum boobs and billiards club?
jokes.setup: Jeff claims to have an invite to a hot new club called 'Single Malt Platinum Boobs and Billiards'
jokes.punchline: Abed reveals he fabricated the club in Photoshop to manipulate Jeff into attending; Jeff's crestfallen question confirms he never questioned the name
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. Abed's methodical manipulation of Jeff is perfectly in character for both — Abed as the hyper-competent planner who anticipated Jeff's narcissism, and Jeff as someone so self-absorbed he never questioned a club called 'Platinum Boobs and Billiards.' Jeff's heartbroken 'I guess I never said it out loud' followed by the dawning realization is beautifully staged. This is craft-forward comedy at its best: the name works as a prop all along, the reveal recontextualizes Jeff's earlier pomposity, and the specific absurdity of the club name is the punchline within the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So what are we doing tonight? Something awesome, right?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're playing board games.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Board games? I thought we were going to do something cool!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Board games are cool.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Can we just go with your original plan instead?

jokes.text: One word, two syllables. Don't say charades. Troy & Abed: Yahtzee! / Is charades off the table?
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed build anticipation with 'one word, two syllables' — classic charades setup language
jokes.punchline: They shout 'Yahtzee!' instead, then Jeff still hopefully asks if charades is off the table — his disappointment revealing he preferred charades despite the buildup being a fake-out
jokes.explanation: Neatly structured misdirection. The charades phrasing is used as a feint, the synchronized shout of Yahtzee is a classic Troy-and-Abed bit, and Jeff's lingering hope for charades adds a character-specific coda. Solid but not spectacular.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what I call Yahtzee? Dice-a-Rooney.

jokes.text: Is there nothing from our youth that these companies won't repackage for a buck? / Call it Yahtzee all you want. Everybody knows it's Puerto Rican chess.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a reasonable cynical observation about repackaging classic games
jokes.punchline: Pierce responds with utter conviction that Yahtzee is 'Puerto Rican chess' — a completely fabricated cultural fact delivered as common knowledge
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce absurdist confidence. The specificity of 'Puerto Rican chess' (why Puerto Rican? why chess?) combined with the absolutism of 'everybody knows' makes this quintessential Pierce — casually racist-adjacent, totally wrong, entirely certain. High character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In an alternate timeline, you rolled a one and got no pizza. In another, you rolled a six and got all the pizza. In infinite other timelines, infinite yous are rolling infinite dice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, I'm just trying to order lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's what they all said.

jokes.text: Just so you know, Jeff, you are now creating six different timelines. / Of course I am, Abed.
jokes.setup: Jeff is about to roll a die to determine who gets the pizza; it's a mundane logistics decision
jokes.punchline: Abed reframes this trivial act in grandiose sci-fi terms; Jeff's dismissive 'Of course I am, Abed' treats this as standard Abed weirdness — which it is, but Abed is also literally correct
jokes.explanation: This is the structural spine of the entire episode — a joke that works on first watch as Abed being his typical genre-aware self, and on rewatch as the literal premise of everything that follows. The genius is in the layering: Jeff's dismissal is both the correct social response AND dramatically ironic given the episode's structure. 'Of course I am, Abed' will be repeated six times, each time gaining meaning. This is exceptionally high-craft comedy writing — a single exchange that is simultaneously the setup, the joke, the episode's thesis, and a running gag. Near the top of the episode's craft ceiling.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa, 'going down'? That's what she said!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Reminds me of the time I was with Eartha Kitt in an airplane bathroom.

jokes.text: Uh, guys? What does a pregnancy test look like? / Like a thin piece of plastic with a thing on the end of it. / Okay, so this is definitely a gun.
jokes.setup: Abed finds something in the bathroom and asks what a pregnancy test looks like, implying he might have found one
jokes.punchline: After getting the description, he concludes it's definitely a gun — the misdirection resolves in the opposite direction from what was set up
jokes.explanation: Beautiful misdirection. The setup feints toward a pregnancy scare (which would fit Annie's anxious character), the description of a pregnancy test matches a gun closely enough that the pivot is funny but logical, and 'okay, so this is definitely a gun' lands with perfect deadpan economy. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing it sets up a whole cascade of events in later timelines (the gun goes off). Very well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It was totally natural.

jokes.text: Oh, my -- Why does Annie have a gun? / That's not a gun, that's a girl's peashooter.
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts in alarm to Annie having a gun
jokes.punchline: Pierce dismisses it as a 'girl's peashooter' — both condescending to Annie and absurdly minimizing a genuine safety hazard
jokes.explanation: Solid Pierce character moment — his casual dismissal of Annie's firearm as a 'girl's peashooter' is exactly the right level of condescending absurdity for his character. Not exceptional but functions well.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What does a pregnancy test look like?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Two pink lines.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, I found a gun.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm gonna get a drink. Ow!' — first instance of Jeff hitting his head on the ceiling fan
jokes.setup: In the first timeline, Jeff steps toward the drink table
jokes.punchline: He immediately hits his head on the ceiling fan — a pratfall that will be repeated across all timelines, becoming both a running gag and a structural device
jokes.explanation: The setup and payoff works on first viewing; on rewatch, knowing this happens in every timeline, it becomes a structural joke about determinism — no matter what, Jeff's vanity and obliviousness gets him clocked by the fan. Good rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: A gun? That's it? I've fought in three wars. I once took down a man with a shoe.

jokes.text: Don't fight over them. Well, y-you can fight a little.
jokes.setup: Pierce gives Troy a housewarming gift (the Norwegian troll) and says not to fight over it
jokes.punchline: He immediately half-retracts, adding 'well, you can fight a little' — revealing he actually wants to cause some conflict
jokes.explanation: Good character beat that reveals Pierce's mischievousness. The 'fight a little' reversal is well-timed. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A man hits his head. It's funny because it hurts and he wasn't expecting it. That's physical comedy in its purest form.

jokes.text: Smells weird. / I beg your pardon? / Smells weird. What did you do? / Abed, you don't ask someone a question like that. It's not dignified.
jokes.setup: Abed emerges from the bathroom and immediately confronts Shirley about an odor
jokes.punchline: He repeats it without apology; Jeff's injunction against asking ('not dignified') implies the question is rude but doesn't deny the smell, making the discomfort worse
jokes.explanation: Abed's social-skills deficit is well-deployed here. His flat repetition of 'smells weird' without acknowledging Shirley's offense, and Jeff's vague injunction against asking (but not denying the smell), creates layered awkward comedy. Good character integration for Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pizza, pizza, in my belly. I love pizza, it's so jelly. Pizza, pizza, on my plate. Pizza makes my taste buds celebrate!

jokes.text: ♪Pizza, pizza, go in tummy / me so hung-ee me so hung-ee♪ / That pizza guy was super creepy. / So you're saying he was a pizza guy?
jokes.setup: The pizza guy apparently sang a disturbing song while delivering the pizza
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response reduces the concern about the man's creepiness to merely confirming his professional identity — implying creepiness is a pizza delivery job requirement
jokes.explanation: Jeff's deadpan 'so you're saying he was a pizza guy?' is a sharp callback-pivot. The pizza song itself is funny (the sung hunger lyric is intentionally awful), and Jeff's response packages the implied joke that pizza delivery guys are universally creepy into one economical line.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He's cute. I wonder if he delivers more than just pizza, if you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't know what you mean. Are you implying he also delivers other food items, or are you making a sexual innuendo?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The second one.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why would a pizza delivery person have access to other people's bodies?

jokes.text: That pizza guy was super creepy. / So you're saying he was a pizza guy?
jokes.setup: Annie reports that the pizza delivery person was extremely creepy
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response implies that pizza delivery guys being creepy is a universal given — the creepiness IS the defining characteristic of the job
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline. The implication that all pizza guys are inherently creepy is a mild observational joke elevated by Jeff's perfect deadpan economy. Not original, but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What if we're not in the prime timeline? What if there's another version of us somewhere making different choices right now?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In one timeline, I'm saying this. In another, I'm not. In another, I'm saying something completely different.

jokes.text: Did you guys know I had sex with Eartha Kitt in an airplane bathroom? / We're about to eat. / It's not namedropping if it comes up organically.
jokes.setup: An unrelated conversation is interrupted by Pierce volunteering a TMI celebrity sex story
jokes.punchline: Pierce defends it as 'not namedropping' because it 'came up organically' — the irony being it did not come up organically at all
jokes.explanation: The first deployment of the Eartha Kitt running gag, which will become funnier with each repetition. Pierce's specific logic — 'it's not namedropping if it comes up organically' — is both self-serving and completely divorced from reality, which is perfect character comedy. The 'we're about to eat' response grounds it in social discomfort. Marks high on character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, we're worried about you. This baking thing has gotten out of hand.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're baking at all hours. It's like a compulsion.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It is NOT a compulsion! I just love baking!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You've baked 47 casseroles this week. That's a compulsion.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well maybe I'm just passionate!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Honey, I've seen addiction. My first three marriages were addictions. This is addiction.

jokes.text: It used to watch me sleep!
jokes.setup: Pierce gifts Troy a Norwegian troll that he claims was displayed outside Troy's bedroom in their shared home — implying Pierce thought Troy was 'taken with' it
jokes.punchline: Troy's traumatized outburst reveals the troll was placed there deliberately by Pierce (creepily) and left Troy disturbed — the gift is suddenly sinister
jokes.explanation: Four words that recontextualize everything Pierce just said. The escalating horror of Pierce having a creepy troll doll watch Troy sleep — and presenting this as a loving gesture — is both funny and deeply unsettling, which is exactly the right comedy register for Pierce. Maximum economy: the entire joke lives in one sentence. Among the most quotable lines in the episode, and gains bonus resonance in the dark timeline where Troy eats it.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That reminds me of the time I met Eartha Kitt in the bathroom of a department store.

jokes.text: Troy: 'It used to watch me sleep!'
jokes.setup: Pierce explains the troll was placed outside Troy's bedroom
jokes.punchline: Troy's traumatized outburst confirms the horror we just inferred — 'it used to watch me sleep!' — delivered with genuine distress
jokes.explanation: Troy's reaction lands perfectly — 'it used to WATCH ME SLEEP' is horrified and specific. The specificity ('used to') implies this was a prolonged experience. High economy, great character integration for Troy's childlike vulnerability.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I was just trying to be helpful!

jokes.text: Did someone remember to take out my pies? [cut to burned pies] Seriously? / Oh! Oh, no. / We weren't gonna eat them. / You're not allowed to have 'baking things' as an identity.
jokes.setup: Shirley's pies have burned; everyone forgot; she's upset
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers the brutal meta-commentary that Shirley isn't 'allowed' to have baking as her identity — voiced as a correction but functioning as a devastating character insight
jokes.explanation: Jeff's line cuts to the thematic heart of Shirley's character arc while still being funny. 'You're not allowed to have baking things as an identity' is a cringe joke that lands as social commentary — the audience laughs uncomfortably because it's both cruel and arguably correct. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I got you something special, Troy. A troll doll. I remember you mentioning how much you loved them.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, no. No, no, no. That's not... I never said I loved trolls. I said I was terrified of them as a child!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, consider this exposure therapy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not how exposure therapy works! And that thing... look at its eyes. It's staring into my soul. This is exactly like the one from my neighbor's house. The one that gave me nightmares for three years.

jokes.text: Excuse me for being the only married woman in a group full of horny toads who sit around all night just making googly eyes at each other. / Googly eyes?
jokes.setup: Shirley defends her baking identity in an outburst
jokes.punchline: Jeff latches onto 'googly eyes' — the specific word choice is funnier than the accusation itself — his confusion/denial landing as both comic deflection and confirmation
jokes.explanation: Jeff's reaction beat on 'googly eyes' is funny but slight. The humor comes from his deflection being so specifically focused on the word rather than the accusation. Works in context, doesn't standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My pies! They're ruined!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, baking isn't a personality.

jokes.text: Nobody makes googly eyes at me either. We're the same.
jokes.setup: Shirley is upset about being ignored romantically within the group
jokes.punchline: Pierce co-opts her pain as solidarity while also inadvertently revealing his own loneliness — 'we're the same' is simultaneously an attempt at comfort and a depressing self-revelation
jokes.explanation: Pierce's attempt at empathy accidentally revealing his own isolation is classic Pierce — he thinks he's offering solidarity but instead reveals how alone he is. The 'we're the same' implies he and the married mother are equally romantically invisible, which is both sad and funny. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You know what? I am a baker. A real baker. And you people are just sexually frustrated children who can't handle a woman with actual skills and confidence.

jokes.text: More like a nervous— / Bakedown! I know! / I didn't say it on purpose.
jokes.setup: Jeff corrects 'more like a nervous—' expecting Abed to complete the sentence with something clever
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'Bakedown' — a pun on 'breakdown' and 'baking' — then disclaims intentionality, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The 'I didn't say it on purpose' coda is what elevates this from a simple pun. Abed's disclaimer is both funny (he seems genuinely uncertain) and in character (Abed's relationship to unintentional humor is different from everyone else's). Jeff's enthusiasm ('I know!') adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Nobody ever asks me out. I'm invisible to men.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hey, I know how you feel. Women won't even look at me anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah. I'm thinking of getting one of those vests that says 'I'm not a threat' on it.

jokes.text: Speaking of crap, I was taking one in an airplane bathroom when Eartha Kitt decided to bang me. / What? It's where my mind went. / Your mind went years ago.
jokes.setup: Second deployment of the Eartha Kitt gag, this time with the added detail that Pierce was using the toilet during the encounter
jokes.punchline: The 'speaking of crap' transition is hilariously forced; Abed's response 'your mind went years ago' is the deadpan kill shot
jokes.explanation: The running gag escalates beautifully — each iteration adds a new grotesque detail. 'Speaking of crap' as a transition is so nakedly forced that it circles back to being funny, and the toilet context makes the story even more preposterous. Abed's response ('your mind went years ago') is uncharacteristically withering for him, which makes it land harder. Best deployment of the Eartha Kitt gag so far.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: She had a nervous break—I mean, she broke down nervously. I wasn't making a pun.

jokes.text: I can't believe those are real mahogany bunk beds in there. I bet that cost you a few allowances.
jokes.setup: Pierce is touring the bedroom and complimenting the bunk beds
jokes.punchline: The 'few allowances' comment infantilizes Troy's adult purchase by framing it in childhood financial terms
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce condescension toward Troy, treating him as a child. Functional but relatively low-impact. The setup is too benign to generate real momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, that reminds me of the time I was with Eartha Kitt in an airplane bathroom. I got to say 'crap' one time.

jokes.text: Um, I was smoking a cigarette. / I know what you were doing. I'm 21 years old. I'm a man.
jokes.setup: Troy walks in on Britta in the bathroom; she offers a cover story about smoking a cigarette (she was clearly doing something more embarrassing — it's the pilot episode of Roxanne)
jokes.punchline: Troy's dignified assertion 'I'm a man' in response to catching Britta doing something private is simultaneously about claiming his maturity and refusing to be embarrassed for either of them
jokes.explanation: Troy's earnest 'I'm a man' is a perfect character beat — he's genuinely trying to assert adult dignity in a mortifying situation. The implication of what Britta was actually doing (mouthing along to 'Roxanne') is funnier because it's so mundane and silly compared to what Troy's knowing tone implies.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's where my mind went.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Your mind is completely gone.

jokes.text: He keeps his toiletries in a safe under the sink.
jokes.setup: Britta is analyzing Jeff's character and what his bathroom choices say about him
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of toiletries in a safe is a perfect absurdist synecdoche for Jeff's entire personality — protecting himself even from imaginary vulnerability
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character-insight comedy. 'He keeps his toiletries in a safe under the sink' is funny on its face, but it's also the most precise possible distillation of Jeff Winger as a character — deeply guarded, trust-deficient, using physical fortifications to protect even mundane personal items. The audience has never seen it but immediately believes it. This is what great character comedy looks like. High marks across the board; among the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is a really nice apartment, Troy. You should be so proud of yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Thanks, Britta. It means a lot coming from you.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I mean, look at you, paying bills, keeping plants alive... here, you've earned this.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Is that... is that a gold star sticker?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You've been such a good boy this month!

jokes.text: Man, pizza guys are getting worse and worse-looking. / Guess all the good ones went into porn. / Ceiling fan. / I miss all the fun.
jokes.setup: The pizza guy has apparently just been seen and found unattractive
jokes.punchline: Pierce's 'all the good ones went into porn' is delivered as genuine social commentary; Jeff's 'ceiling fan' is a non sequitur that reveals he hit his head on something above him
jokes.explanation: Pierce's porn observation is characteristically bawdy but not especially inventive. Jeff's 'ceiling fan' is a funny visual gag (inferring he's hit his head) but undersold in text form. The 'I miss all the fun' coda is a nice cap. Functional but weak by this episode's standards.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta? What are you doing in here?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Nothing! I was just... washing my hands.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Your hands are dry.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Look, I'm mature enough to handle whatever this is.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I was practicing my acceptance speech for a Peabody Award.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You were singing Beyoncé in the mirror again, weren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: You know what's great? Air travel. I've flown a lot, a lot of airplane stories. I once had sex with Eartha Kitt— / Okay, I'm gonna check on my pies.
jokes.setup: Third timeline; Pierce is about to launch into the Eartha Kitt story again when Shirley pre-emptively leaves
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately exits at the first mention of Eartha Kitt — she's heard enough in the other timelines (or at least once) to know what's coming
jokes.explanation: The running gag's third deployment works because it now shows Pierce telegraphing the story so obviously that Shirley bails before he finishes the sentence. The escalating pattern of avoidance is satisfying structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You've got your own apartment, you pay your own bills, you even have little olives in your bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Those are for my toilet.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know what they're for, Troy. That's fancy.

jokes.text: Do I need to refill the toilet olives? / We're good, I checked. / You're the best.
jokes.setup: In passing, the apartment's bathroom amenities are referenced
jokes.punchline: Troy confirms he has already checked on the 'toilet olives' — implying (1) olives in the bathroom is normal for their apartment, (2) they're a standard hospitality item, (3) Troy has been responsibly monitoring them
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Toilet olives' is established, confirmed, and praised in three lines with zero explanation — the show trusts you to find the absurdity yourself. The fact that Troy has CHECKED on them and Abed says 'you're the best' treats this as a solemn hospitality duty. The lack of anyone finding this odd is the joke. Exceptional economy and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, why do you need three locks on the bathroom door?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's called privacy, Troy. Some of us value our personal space.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Three locks? That's not privacy, that's a panic room. What are you doing in there, defusing a bomb?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I also installed a keypad. And security cameras.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Security cameras? In the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Only pointing inward. For my own records.

jokes.text: Do I need to refill the toilet olives? / We're good. I checked. / You're the best.
jokes.setup: Abed asks a maintenance question during a tense emotional moment
jokes.punchline: 'Toilet olives' — the apartment has a bowl of olives next to the toilet, treated with complete normalcy as a standard amenity requiring refilling
jokes.explanation: The 'toilet olives' callback is handled beautifully — first mentioned as a character-defining detail about Troy, now treated as a household responsibility. The matter-of-fact delivery ('I checked') and the warm response ('you're the best') normalize the absurdity completely, which is the funniest possible treatment.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, with looks like that, you should be doing porn, not delivering pizzas.

jokes.text: Want to stay up all night talking in our bunk beds? / Duh-doy.
jokes.setup: Abed proposes staying up talking in their bunk beds
jokes.punchline: 'Duh-doy' — Troy's invented word for an obvious yes, delivered with zero hesitation
jokes.explanation: One word carrying enormous character weight. 'Duh-doy' is entirely Troy — a childlike enthusiastic affirmative that shows his genuine excitement about their friendship. Perfectly economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm an adult. I can stab whoever I want.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, you can't.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I said so.

jokes.text: Feel the terror! Stop the tantrum! Feel the terror of the Norwegian troll!
jokes.setup: Pierce is apparently chasing or terrorizing Troy with the troll doll in the bedroom
jokes.punchline: Pierce narrating his own attack ('feel the terror!') like a villain in a children's show while doing it makes the act both more ridiculous and more revealing of his loneliness
jokes.explanation: Pierce self-narrating his troll attack is unhinged and very funny. The childishness of the act paired with his pompous vocabulary ('Stop the tantrum!') creates characteristic Pierce absurdity. His jealousy over the Troy/Abed friendship being expressed through literal toy violence is simultaneously sad and hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You can't escape me, Troy! I am the master of this troll doll, and you are its prey!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, please! Just put it down!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Never! The troll has spoken, and its hunger knows no bounds!

jokes.text: Hey, guys, this is Toby, our pizza delivery guy. And I know this is gonna sound nuts, but we're in love and we're getting married.
jokes.setup: Everyone has been waiting for the pizza; Britta has gone to get it
jokes.punchline: Britta has fallen in love with and agreed to marry the pizza delivery man within the span of a pizza delivery — presented with earnest sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest payoffs. Britta's impulsive anarchist personality taken to its logical extreme: she falls in love and gets engaged to the pizza guy in the time it takes to descend a staircase. The deadpan 'I know this is gonna sound nuts' acknowledgment followed by the completely nuts statement is perfect structure. Entirely in character for Britta as the group's self-sabotaging wild card. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I went to get pizza and somehow got instantly engaged to the creepy pizza guy.

jokes.text: I wonder what happened in all those other timelines. / Wait, there are other timelines?
jokes.setup: Abed as usual muses about alternate timelines; in this timeline, Britta is apparently unaware of Abed's earlier declaration
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'Wait, there are other timelines?' — in the timeline where she just returned engaged to a pizza guy — is the most perfect possible response from the least self-aware character
jokes.explanation: The fact that Britta — having just announced her engagement to a pizza delivery person — is newly curious about alternate timelines is an excellent structural joke. Her priorities are perfectly upside down.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I wonder what I'm doing in other timelines. Like, in one timeline, I'm probably a really successful film director.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: In another timeline, you're probably dead.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Thanks, Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious. You should be careful. There are infinite versions of you, and statistically, most of them are probably dead.

jokes.text: You know who I used to call miss anything? Eartha Kitt. / What? He totally set me up.
jokes.setup: Troy's line about not missing anything triggers Pierce's Eartha Kitt obsession
jokes.punchline: Pierce's forced pun ('miss anything' → 'Miss Kitt') followed by his fourth-wall defense 'he totally set me up' — Pierce breaks the fourth wall to claim the joke was earned
jokes.explanation: The best deployment of the Eartha Kitt gag. Pierce's wordplay (forced as it is) is at least structurally justified this time, and his self-defense to the audience ('he totally set me up') is a moment of genuine meta-awareness from a character who is usually oblivious. The escalating nature of the gag combined with Pierce's defensive self-awareness makes this the most rewarding iteration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Troy sings while Pierce is dying in the burning apartment

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Pierce makes final commentary while flames consume the room

jokes.text: The gun going off — 'No! Call 911! Abed, help me stop the bleeding! / I'm dying! / Pierce. / I am dying.'
jokes.setup: In Timeline 1 (Troy goes to get pizza), the gun Annie brought falls or is mishandled
jokes.punchline: Pierce gets shot in the leg; his dramatic insistence 'I am dying' — corrected gravity emphasis — is played for dark comedy as the most extreme possible consequence of the die roll
jokes.explanation: The darkest timeline reveal — Pierce getting shot from a dropped gun is an excellent escalation of the apartment party stakes. The comic-tragic framing (Pierce insisting 'I AM dying' with strange emphasis on 'am') is pitch-perfect. The whole sequence demonstrates how the show uses dark consequences for genuine comedy without undercutting the absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, these taste like regular pies.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: They're mini pies, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know, but they taste like full-size pies. How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It's the same recipe, just smaller portions.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is witchcraft.

jokes.text: I'm dying! / Pierce. / I am dying.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been shot in the leg; he's dramatically declaring he's dying
jokes.punchline: Abed gently, flatly says 'Pierce' — not to comfort him, but as a soft correction; Pierce doubles down: 'I am dying' — his refusal to accept medical fact or Abed's correction
jokes.explanation: Pierce's melodramatic self-diagnosis undercut by Abed's one-word reality check is very well-timed. The doubling down on 'I am dying' after the correction is perfectly Pierce — he's constitutionally unable to retreat from a dramatic position.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, I wasn't supposed to mention the no-pie pact.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What no-pie pact?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. We also agreed never to eat ice cream on Tuesdays.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And we may have made a blood oath about pudding.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're spiraling.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: There's also the thing about the methamphetamine lab in the study room!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

jokes.text: ♪You don't have to put on the red light♪ ... Water. Water! Water!
jokes.setup: In the darkest timeline, the apartment descends into chaos — Pierce is shot, Roxanne is playing
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of Britta's singing 'Roxanne' with people screaming 'Water!' as the apartment apparently burns creates surreal comedic horror
jokes.explanation: The chaos of the darkest timeline is played as dark comedy rather than drama. The specific choice to have 'Roxanne' as the soundtrack to disaster is perfect — Britta singing while the apartment burns is simultaneously absurd and in character. Works better visually than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, my boy, I want to give you something special. How about a lifetime supply of turtle necks?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No? Okay, okay, I've got it - a jet ski. A jet ski for the library.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Still no? Fine, fine, I'm thinking bigger now. What about my collection of vintage pornographic playing cards?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: A solid gold toilet seat with your initials engraved in it?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My old toupee collection? I've got seventeen of them, Jeff. Seventeen!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What if I just... gave you a year's supply of expired mayonnaise? I've got it in the freezer.

jokes.text: Everybody give me money. / Wow, that ascot really softens your personality.
jokes.setup: Pierce is wearing an ascot in the fifth timeline
jokes.punchline: The observation that the ascot 'softens his personality' implies that without it Pierce is even sharper/worse, which is both a compliment and an insult
jokes.explanation: Decent visual/character joke — an ascot as Pierce's personality-softening garment is appropriately absurd. 'Softens your personality' as a backhanded compliment works. Not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You're a drug addict, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not a drug addict. I'm a baker. I just sold some brownies to a guy behind the library for fifty bucks.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He said they were 'life-changing.' I'm thinking of expanding my operation.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. They taste just like regular-size pies.
jokes.setup: Shirley offers mini pies; someone (or Shirley herself) reacts with amazement
jokes.punchline: The discovery that mini pies taste like regular pies presented as a revelation — the implicit joke being that this is not a discovery at all
jokes.explanation: Mild absurdist/deadpan gag. The 'discovery' that mini pies taste like pies is funny because of the earnestness of the amazement, but it's a small joke in a small moment.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm watching you two, and Jeff, your technique is very textbook. Very... by-the-book. Annie, you're doing that thing where you're thinking too hard. I can see it happening. You're literally thinking during the kiss. Also, Jeff, your jaw is too tense. Relax your jaw.

jokes.text: Sometimes I feel like making desserts is the only thing I'm good for in the group.
jokes.setup: Abed and Shirley have a quiet moment; she opens up
jokes.punchline: Shirley's vulnerability becomes a joke because it's both true (from the group's perspective) and self-aware — she's naming the exact dynamic the episode has been examining, which produces dark, uncomfortable laughter
jokes.explanation: More dark-comedy-adjacent than pure laugh. Shirley's self-aware lament works because the audience knows she's right and the episode has been making that joke all episode. The irony is that the character saying it treats it as tragedy while the audience hears it as a knowing confession.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You know what, Pierce? You're a terrible person!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from you, you sanctimonious hypocrite!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: At least I don't spend all day making racist comments and thinking I'm hilarious!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And at least I don't hide behind religion to judge everyone while being just as awful!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You're a fossil! A walking, talking relic from an era nobody misses!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're a shrill, obnoxious busybody who nobody actually likes!

jokes.text: Crap. I was not supposed to eat your stuff. We all made an agreement. / Crap, I was not supposed to say that out loud! / Crap, okay, cards on the table, I'm really high right now.
jokes.setup: Pierce has eaten Shirley's pie (which was apparently marijuana-laced) and begins confessing in a cascade of unintended revelations
jokes.punchline: Three 'crap' moments of escalating candor — each confession triggering the next — culminating in the full admission of being high
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent escalation comedy. The repeated 'crap' as a beat that introduces each new confession creates a perfect rhythm — the audience starts anticipating the next 'crap' by the third one. Each level of honesty is funnier than the last because Pierce's attempt to control his confessions keeps making them worse. The final revelation ('I'm really high') recontextualizes everything and raises the question of what's in the pies. Among the episode's better-structured jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I wonder what happened in the timeline where I found twenty dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? I found twenty dollars!

jokes.text: No, I wanna give you something else. / A waterpik! / A speedboat! Two waterpiks.
jokes.setup: Shirley is furious at Pierce for eating her (presumably marijuana-laced) pies; Pierce high and panicking tries to offer alternative gifts
jokes.punchline: The gifts escalate from mundane to insane to doubling back — 'a waterpik' is funny, 'a speedboat' is funnier, 'two waterpiks' as a de-escalation is the perfect absurdist punctuation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The escalation structure is immaculate: a mundane gift (waterpik) → an absurdly large gift (speedboat) → a retreat to double the mundane (two waterpiks). The de-escalation is the genius move — going back to the waterpik but multiplying it is funnier than any further escalation would have been. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted verbatim. Pierce's high desperation + the gifts' internal logic is perfect character comedy. Near the top of the episode's impact scores.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You can't roll the die, Jeff. Not because of the rules, but because chaos isn't something you control—it's something you accept. And right now, the only thing more chaotic than a die roll is a group of people who've learned to care about each other despite everything telling them not to. That's the real roll. That's what matters.

jokes.text: Stop. A little Make Out 101. Less dad talk. And, uh, you could ease up on the bubblegum lip gloss.
jokes.setup: High Jeff and Annie are having a moment; she brings up her dad, undermining the romantic tension
jokes.punchline: Jeff — still high — tries to give Annie kissing notes ('Make Out 101') while criticizing her lip gloss, which is simultaneously inappropriate and deeply Jeff
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'Make Out 101' critique while high — including a specific complaint about bubblegum lip gloss — is perfect character comedy. His coaching of Annie's romantic behavior is both inappropriate and revealing of his actual feelings, wrapped in affected nonchalance.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what I love about our group? We're predictable. In the best way. Jeff does something selfish, we call him out, he has a moment of growth, and we all hug it out. It's beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I calculated every variable in that equation to make sure I'd come out on top.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. Predictable.

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm feeding my pies to a drug addict! / Drug addict? You're a pie pusher! You push pies to get love.
jokes.setup: Shirley is furious that Pierce ate her marijuana-laced pies
jokes.punchline: Pierce counter-attacks with 'pie pusher' — recasting Shirley's baking compulsion as drug-dealer behavior — and the meta-analysis 'you push pies to get love' is both absurdly accurate and devastating
jokes.explanation: Pierce's high state gives him accidental insight that he'd never deliver sober. 'Pie pusher' is a perfect portmanteau insult, and 'you push pies to get love' lands as simultaneously comic and genuinely perceptive — it's the truest thing Pierce says in the episode. The irony that this comes from Pierce in a drug-addled state is delicious. High on character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not manipulating you guys. I'm just... strategically leveraging our friendship for mutual benefit.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And honestly, that's what friendship is about. It's like that song says: 'You scratch my back, I'll scratch yours.' Classic friendship anthem.

jokes.text: Give it, Pierce! / It feels fun!
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are physically fighting over something (the gun? a pie?)
jokes.punchline: Pierce's mid-struggle declaration 'it feels fun!' is an utterly un-self-conscious expression of pure id — he's high, fighting, and enjoying it
jokes.explanation: 'It feels fun!' is four syllables of pure Pierce. His high-state confession of enjoying something he shouldn't be doing is completely unguarded and therefore funny. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What's wrong with you? You're like an airplane bathroom—small, cramped, and full of crap.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's it! That reminds me of the time I was in an airplane bathroom with Eartha Kitt!

jokes.text: Give me this, you godless hippie skank! / You're a sick, sad, twisted old man. And I hope you die alone.
jokes.setup: The fight between Shirley and Pierce has escalated to full mutual insult exchange
jokes.punchline: Both characters reach for their most character-specific insults — Shirley's 'godless hippie skank' targets Britta (Pierce has apparently redirected), and Pierce's existential curse ('I hope you die alone') is somehow the more vulnerable statement
jokes.explanation: Both insults are character-specific and land well. Shirley's religious phrasing ('godless') and her specific targeting is funny. The irony that 'I hope you die alone' from Pierce is probably projection — he's the most likely to die alone — adds dark resonance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is actually pretty great, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know, right? No conflicts, no drama.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We should do this more often!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is like a musical montage sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Everyone singing together in perfect harmony!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Hallelujah! This is what I've been praying for!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Even I'm not ruining this with something inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Group
dialogue.line: *singing and dancing together*

jokes.text: I gotta say, I hope this is the real one, because I just found a nickel in the hallway.
jokes.setup: After witnessing all the chaos of a timeline where things went badly, Abed is reflecting on which timeline is real
jokes.punchline: Abed's criteria for hoping this is the 'real' timeline is finding a nickel — a mundane, tiny positive event set against apocalyptic context
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's very best lines. Abed is the only character who understands the full timeline mechanics, and the joke is that his investment in the 'real' timeline is pegged to the most mundane possible good fortune — a nickel. The understatement is perfect: surrounded by chaos and genuine human suffering across timelines, Abed's optimism is calibrated to twelve-and-a-half-cents-worth of luck. Near-perfect economy and character integration. This is what deadpan understatement looks like at its peak.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're like a TV show that just lost its weirdest character. Now we're just a standard ensemble drama waiting to get cancelled.

jokes.text: Annie will always be driven. Shirley will always be giving. Pierce will never apologize. Britta's sort of a wild card from my perspective. And Jeff will forever remain a conniving son-of-a-bitch.
jokes.setup: Abed gives an earnest speech about the group's strengths and how they hold them together
jokes.punchline: The speech builds genuinely toward Jeff — then 'conniving son-of-a-bitch' lands as a devastating character summary delivered with the same warm sincerity as the other compliments; 'Britta's sort of a wild card' is also a perfect aside
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's crown jewels. The setup is a genuine heartfelt speech about the group's virtues — 'driven,' 'giving' — and Abed delivers each with analytical sincerity. The Britta aside ('sort of a wild card from my perspective') is beautifully hedged — even Abed's data can't predict her. Then 'conniving son-of-a-bitch' for Jeff lands with maximum impact because (a) it's entirely accurate, (b) Abed delivers it with the same earnest tone as the compliments, and (c) the group's reaction immediately follows. This is craft-level joke writing: the structure is a compliment machine that fires one insult in perfect position. The character integration is as high as it gets — only Abed could deliver this speech this way.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In this timeline, there was a fire in the blanket fort.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why don't we just put it out with more fire?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not how fire works, Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not a scientist!

jokes.text: He devised a system by which he never has to get the pizza. / Jeff! / Really? Dang, man. / You crafty jackrabbit. / Asshole. / Pretty low, dude. / It's called friendship, look it up. Encarta it.
jokes.setup: Abed reveals Jeff has been rolling the die starting from the left so the number will never land on him (he's the last in the sequence of seven with a six-sided die)
jokes.punchline: Jeff's unapologetic defense: 'It's called friendship, look it up. Encarta it.' — defiant redefinition of selfishness as friendship, with 'Encarta' as a dated search-engine joke
jokes.explanation: Jeff's unrepentant response to being exposed is classic Jeff. 'Encarta it' as a substitution for 'Google it' is a perfectly Jeff-flavored joke — he uses an outdated reference with total confidence. The cascade of different-voiced condemnations ('Dang, man,' 'You crafty jackrabbit,' 'Asshole') each in distinct character voices is a good ensemble moment. High on character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You can't just eat a troll like that. You need to think strategically.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? This is exactly how you eat a troll. You go in fast, catch it off guard, and—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Look, I've done this before, okay? The key is you want to get the troll when it's vulnerable. If you hesitate, it's going to turn on you.

jokes.text: Oh, like it matters who goes. / [immediately hits head on ceiling fan] / What's so funny? / Karma.
jokes.setup: Jeff dismisses the pizza-getting unfairness; then immediately injures himself
jokes.punchline: The instant physical punishment for Jeff's self-serving speech, followed by Shirley's one-word verdict: 'Karma'
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing in script form. Jeff's dismissal of fairness is immediately and divinely punished, and Shirley's one-word 'Karma' is the ideal response — morally satisfied, economical, and in complete character for Shirley's religiosity. The fact that Jeff has been hitting his head on the fan across multiple timelines makes this the final karmic accounting of that running gag. Excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Our lives have gotten pretty dark.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I dyed my hair black.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I lost my arm.

jokes.text: That guy sucks harder than the toilet in an airplane bathroom. / Airplane bathroom... / Oh, my pies!
jokes.setup: Someone says 'airplane bathroom' in context; Pierce hears the trigger words
jokes.punchline: Pierce starts to respond to the Eartha Kitt trigger but Shirley immediately derails by remembering her pies — the running gag is hijacked by the other running gag
jokes.explanation: Meta-joke where two running gags collide and cancel each other out. Pierce gearing up for his Eartha Kitt story being interrupted by Shirley's pie panic is structurally elegant — the audience has the pleasure of anticipating the gag and then having it subverted. Good economy of comedic real estate.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We could become evil versions of ourselves.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How? Evil goatees?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We'd need practical evil accessories. I'm thinking eye patches with growing instructions.

jokes.text: ♪ Roxanne ♪ — plays as chaos erupts: Shirley screams, the troll catches fire, 'Sing, Britta!' / 'I really love your place. You should move here.'
jokes.setup: Roxanne begins playing as the apartment descends into chaos — troll catches fire, pies burn
jokes.punchline: In the middle of disaster, Annie tells Jeff 'I really love your place. You should move here' — a callback to Jeff's earlier comment about the apartment, now delivered with absurd inappropriate timing
jokes.explanation: The climactic convergence of all running gags (Roxanne, troll, pies, Shirley, Britta singing) is well-orchestrated. The 'Sing, Britta!' moment callbacks her singing history. Annie's casually timed apartment pitch in the middle of chaos is a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You can't just manipulate people like that! Do you have any idea how evil that is?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, it's not evil. It's morally gray.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's EVIL, Abed!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Evil has a specific definition. This is more of a chaotic neutral situation.

jokes.text: I really love your place. You should move here.
jokes.setup: Jeff is apparently looking around the apartment appreciatively — speaking to Annie
jokes.punchline: Jeff expressing a desire for Annie to live with him, delivered while in someone else's apartment he's also enjoying — he's managing to be charming and completely self-serving simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Mild flirtatious Jeff line. Character-consistent but not especially inventive. The dual meaning (he likes the apartment and also maybe wants Annie closer) is there but understated to the point of not quite landing as a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey Abed, you know what this calls for?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Our jingle?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Our jingle.

dialogue.speaker: Troy and Abed
dialogue.line: Troy and Abed in the moooorning! (Evil laugh) In the morning!

jokes.text: To Pierce. May he rest in Pierce.
jokes.setup: In the dark timeline, Pierce has apparently died; the group is toasting him
jokes.punchline: 'May he rest in Pierce' — substituting his name for 'peace' in the standard funeral toast, delivered with Abed's total deadpan
jokes.explanation: Five words. Perfect economy. The pun is obvious but the delivery context — Abed delivering a funeral toast with complete sincerity in a show about alternate timelines — makes it land harder than a simple pun should. It's both a genuinely good pun AND a character moment (only Abed would phrase it this way) AND dark comedy (Pierce really died). One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Shirley, don't you think you've had enough? / Of you.
jokes.setup: In the darkest timeline, Shirley has become a drunk; Abed comments on her drinking
jokes.punchline: Shirley's 'Of you' — she interprets the question as asking if she's had enough of Abed — is a classic drunk's deflection that's also genuinely funny as a character inversion
jokes.explanation: Two words doing enormous work. Shirley-the-drunk deflecting with 'Of you' is both a great character inversion (the warmest member becomes the most hostile) and a funny standalone comeback. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Shirley, don't you think you've had enough? / Of you.
jokes.setup: Jeff expresses concern about Shirley drinking too much in the dark timeline
jokes.punchline: 'Of you.' — Shirley redirects the 'had enough' phrase back at Jeff himself, refusing his authority
jokes.explanation: Two-word comeback that recontextualizes the question. Shirley drunk and defiant toward Jeff is a character-reversal that's funny, and 'Of you' as the redirect is maximally economical. Good entry-level deadpan.

jokes.text: Abed catalogs the darkest timeline: 'Pierce got shot in the leg and died. Shirley's a drunk. Annie's locked in a mental ward because her guilt drove her insane. Jeff lost an arm in the fire. Troy lost his larynx because, for some dumb reason, he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it.'
jokes.setup: Abed summarizes the catastrophic consequences of Troy going to get the pizza (Timeline 5)
jokes.punchline: Each character's fate escalates in absurdity — Pierce dying from a leg wound is bad; Troy destroying a troll by eating it is so specific and illogical that it circles back to funny. 'For some dumb reason' is Abed's editorial commentary.
jokes.explanation: The darkest timeline catalog is excellent escalation comedy. The fates become progressively more specific and absurd — the troll-eating detail is the peak because it's so illogically specific that only Troy would do it. 'For some dumb reason' is Abed at his most revealing: even in the darkest timeline, he maintains editorial distance and judges Troy's troll-eating strategy. High marks.

jokes.text: Pierce got shot in the leg and died. Shirley's a drunk. Annie's locked in a mental ward because her guilt drove her insane. Jeff lost an arm in the fire. Troy lost his larynx because, for some dumb reason, he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it.
jokes.setup: Abed catalogs the catastrophic consequences of the darkest timeline
jokes.punchline: Each character's fate escalates in darkness, culminating in Troy's fate — losing his larynx because 'for some dumb reason he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it' — the dumbest, most specific, funniest possible darkest-timeline fate
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's greatest jokes. The escalating catalog of disasters is excellent, but Troy's fate is the masterpiece: 'for some dumb reason, he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it.' The editorial 'for some dumb reason' — delivered by Abed with mild exasperation — acknowledges that even in the darkest timeline, this was a questionable strategy. All the running gags (troll, fire, Roxanne) converge in this one fate. Exceptional originality, structure, and character integration.

jokes.text: Pierce got shot in the leg and died! Shirley's a drunk. Annie's locked in a mental ward because her guilt drove her insane. Jeff lost an arm in the fire. Troy lost his larynx because, for some dumb reason, he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it.
jokes.setup: Abed is cataloguing the damage done in the darkest timeline to explain why they need to fix things
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from tragic to absurd — specifically 'Troy lost his larynx because, for some dumb reason, he tried to destroy a flaming troll doll by eating it' — the mundane logical caveat ('for some dumb reason') applied to a completely insane act
jokes.explanation: The pinnacle of the episode's dark comedy. Abed's matter-of-fact list of catastrophes builds in absurdity until the Troy entry makes the room erupt. 'For some dumb reason' is the killer — Abed is simultaneously baffled by Troy's logic and offering the most understated possible comment on eating a flaming object. The fact that it's Troy (the most childlike character) doing this for the most Troy-possible reason (he thought eating it would destroy the troll, like a logic only a child would follow) makes it perfect character comedy. The callback to the troll doll from earlier in the episode is earned. This is very close to the best joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Clearly you don't understand anything about defeating trolls.
jokes.setup: Abed has just explained that Troy destroyed his own larynx trying to eat a flaming troll doll
jokes.punchline: Troy, without any self-awareness or irony, defends his decision by asserting that the method was sound — 'you don't understand anything about defeating trolls' implies there IS a correct way
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. Troy's response — delivered without larynx, presumably raspy and damaged — defends the fundamental premise of his action. 'Clearly you don't understand anything about defeating trolls' implies (a) there IS a canonical way to defeat trolls, (b) Troy knows it, and (c) he executed it correctly. The total absence of self-awareness is perfect Troy characterization. The line could only come from this character and no one else. It recontextualizes Abed's 'for some dumb reason' as Abed being the one who doesn't understand troll-defeating methodology. This is the kind of line that becomes a cultural touchstone for the show's fans. Exceptional originality, structure, and character integration.

jokes.text: Life has gone to hell, Abed. This is real! Look at us. Look at me! / Britta, you put one wash-away blue streak in your hair. / And I lost an arm. / Exactly. Life got dark.
jokes.setup: Britta is giving a passionate speech about how terrible their lives have become in the dark timeline
jokes.punchline: Abed's rebuttal to 'look at me!' is simply noting she has one wash-away blue streak — implying her contribution to the 'darkness' is entirely reversible and cosmetic; Britta's 'and I lost an arm' is her counter, and Abed's flat 'exactly' treats both changes as equivalent evidence
jokes.explanation: A masterpiece of comic deflation. Britta's dramatic 'Look at me!' gets met with the most minor possible observation (a wash-away streak), and when she escalates with the genuinely dark 'and I lost an arm,' Abed's 'exactly' treats the missing arm as equivalent to the hair streak in terms of diagnostic significance. The joke works because Abed is treating both data points as equal evidence — which is both wrong and somehow logically consistent from his perspective. This is 'Snip, snap!' level escalation-and-deflation comedy. Very high craft.

jokes.text: Of all the timelines, this is clearly the darkest, which is why I propose we commit to being evil. I made us all black goatees out of felt. I suggest you put them on until you're able to grow your own.
jokes.setup: Abed announces the group should commit to evil as a solution to their dark timeline situation
jokes.punchline: The 'evil' plan is signified by felt goatees — a direct parody of the Star Trek 'Mirror, Mirror' trope where evil counterparts have goatees; Abed treats the felt goatees as a literal practical solution with the qualifier 'until you're able to grow your own'
jokes.explanation: Peak Abed comedy. The felt goatee plan is a brilliant synthesis of Abed's pop-culture brain — taking the Star Trek evil-doppelganger visual shorthand completely literally and implementing it as a genuine strategy. 'Until you're able to grow your own' is the killer addendum — it treats the felt goatees as temporary practical measures rather than symbolic jokes, which makes them funnier. Only Abed could conceive of, construct, and earnestly propose this plan. Extremely high character integration.

jokes.text: Evil Abed. / Mm-hm? / As evil Jeff, am I allowed to pull fewer punches with you? / Certainly. / I hate you!
jokes.setup: Jeff has accepted the 'evil Jeff' identity; he wants to test the new social rules
jokes.punchline: Jeff's big evil declaration is 'I hate you!' — the tamest possible evil statement, funny because evil Jeff's cruelest impulse is so mild, and also because Jeff actually might mean it a little
jokes.explanation: Good comic beat. The formal permission structure ('am I allowed to pull fewer punches?') followed by the pathetically small punch ('I hate you!') is a nice deflation. Abed's 'Certainly' is perfectly solemn.

jokes.text: Shut up with your Sci-Fi crap! I lost my damn arm, and you're making fake beards! / Goatees.
jokes.setup: Jeff breaks from the evil bit to express genuine frustration about the goatee plan
jokes.punchline: Abed's correction 'Goatees' — not responding to the substance of Jeff's complaint at all, only correcting the descriptor — is perfect Abed priority inversion
jokes.explanation: One of the purest character jokes in the episode. Jeff is genuinely furious and in pain — he's lost an arm, he's in a nightmare timeline — and Abed's only response to the entire emotional outburst is a terminology correction. 'Goatees.' One word. Perfect character integration: Abed doesn't dismiss Jeff's pain, he simply doesn't process it because he's focused on accuracy. The economy is flawless. This is exactly the kind of joke that makes Abed as a character work — his precision is simultaneously frustrating and kind of admirable.

jokes.text: ♪Evil Troy and Evil Abed♪
jokes.setup: The evil versions of Troy and Abed, in the darkest timeline, end the scene
jokes.punchline: They sing their apartment jingle but with 'Evil' prepended — the warm, silly opening gag is now in minor key, as it were; the same sincerity now feels menacing and sad simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural callbacks in the episode. The jingle from the opening — a pure expression of Troy and Abed's childlike joy — returns as 'Evil Troy and Evil Abed' sung with the same earnestness, but now marking a tragedy. The joke works in multiple registers: (1) it's funny that evil versions of them still sing the jingle, (2) the juxtaposition of the warm melody with 'evil' is incongruous, (3) it shows their bond persists even in the worst timeline, and (4) it's a perfect structural callback that rewards attentive viewers. Among the highest-craft moments of the episode.

jokes.text: What's wrong? / I don't know. / I guess nothing.
jokes.setup: Back in the 'real' timeline after all the chaos, Jeff and Abed have a quiet moment; Jeff seems vaguely unsettled
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'I guess nothing' after 'I don't know' — the absence of a specific problem being both literally true (nothing bad happened in this timeline) and emotionally hollow; the joke is in the gap between what the audience has seen and what Jeff has experienced
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the episode. Jeff's vague unease ('I don't know... I guess nothing') is funny because the audience has watched five timelines of disaster while he only experienced one evening. The deadpan understatement is the episode's quiet final joke — nothing is wrong, and yet everything could have been. Good economy and structural elegance as a closing beat.

tmdb_overview: When Jeff introduces an element of randomness into Troy and Abed's housewarming party, reality splits into six timelines.
insight: Six timelines spawn 65 jokes in 42 minutes — Community's most ambitious structural comedy.
